entries.name: Adaptive Metropolis
entries.definition: A history-adaptive random-walk Metropolis sampler whose Gaussian proposal covariance is estimated from the accumulated retained states, including repetitions after rejected proposals.
entries.identity_notes: This record identifies covariance adaptation from the full retained history, distinguished from a fixed random-walk kernel, finite sliding-window adaptation, scale-only tuning and RAM direction-based adaptation. The original empirical-covariance form and later recursive modifications share this core but differ in update timing and regularization. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 181 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive searches of both full checkouts found prior discovery leads, neighboring sampler discussions and unrelated author-name/environment substrings. Existing random-walk Metropolis, delayed-rejection, fixed symmetric delayed-rejection and RAM records were inspected; shared components do not make these procedures equivalent.
entries.mechanism: Start at a state with positive target density. In the original form, after an initial period with a chosen positive-definite C0, propose Y from N(X_(t−1), C_t), where C_t=s_d[Cov(X_0,...,X_(t−1))+epsilon I], epsilon>0 and s_d>0. The empirical covariance uses every retained state, with denominator t−1 for t available states; choose the adaptation start after at least two states. Accept with min(1,pi(Y)/pi(X_(t−1))) and otherwise repeat the old state. The fixed-covariance Metropolis rule is used at each iteration, but adapting C_t from the sampled history requires a separate validity argument.
entries.locator: Section 5, Equations (26)–(30), PDF pp. 14–15, and Theorem 10, pp. 15–16; compare original 2001 Section 2, Equations (1)–(2), printed pp. 224–226
limitations: The 2010 source explicitly analyzes a recursive modification, not an exact restatement of the original unbiased sample covariance. Its displayed outline also shifts the covariance index; the original timing is stated explicitly here.

The original full-method text was read through a public indexed PDF. Direct download returned 403 and no visible page images were obtained; no original-PDF hash or visual inspection is claimed. The 2010 method pages were read and visually checked.
The original bounded-support result and the later regular superexponential-tail results have different hypotheses. Neither licenses arbitrary targets or unrestricted adaptive variants.

The usual dimension-based scale is a tuning heuristic under particular target assumptions, not a universal optimum. Empirical covariance estimation can be unsuitable for distributions without finite second moments.
The sampled-state sequence alone is history dependent; invariant kernels at frozen settings do not by themselves prove adaptive convergence.

entries.name: Delayed-rejection adaptive Metropolis
entries.definition: An adaptive Metropolis procedure combining history-based Gaussian proposal covariance updates between transitions with corrected delayed-rejection proposal stages within a transition.
entries.identity_notes: DRAM combines two distinct mechanisms: retained-history covariance learning across iterations and reversed-path acceptance corrections for additional attempts after rejection. The inspected author implementation supplies the explicit Gaussian-stage realization; it is not merely repeated ordinary Metropolis tests. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 181 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive searches of both full checkouts found prior discovery leads, neighboring sampler discussions and unrelated author-name/environment substrings. Existing random-walk Metropolis, delayed-rejection, fixed symmetric delayed-rejection and RAM records were inspected; shared components do not make these procedures equivalent.
entries.mechanism: At fixed proposal settings for a transition, first propose y1 from N(x,C1) and use the Metropolis target ratio. After rejection propose y2 from N(x,C2), centered at the original x, with C2=C1/d1² for a positive stage scale d1 (d1>1 narrows the proposal). Let q_i(a,b) denote the Gaussian proposal density at b from a and a1(a,b)=min(1,pi(b)/pi(a)). On a reachable rejection path, accept y2 with min(1, [pi(y2)q1(y2,y1)q2(y2,x)(1−a1(y2,y1))]/[pi(x)q1(x,y1)q2(x,y2)(1−a1(x,y1))]). Higher stages use the recursive forward/reverse rejection products and earlier-stage Gaussian proposal ratios. Retain x after all capped stages reject. At scheduled iterations, update the empirical covariance from stored retained states including repeats, scale its Cholesky factor, and recompute stage factors for later transitions. In the inspected implementation diagonal jitter is attempted only when factorization fails; if that attempt also fails, the previous proposal factor is retained.
entries.locator: mcmcrun.m lines 119–168 (method controls), 339–380 (factors), 497–603 (proposals and retained chain), 661–717 (covariance adaptation), 854–905 (alphafun, qfun, lfun)
limitations: The original 2006 article metadata was located but its complete method PDF was not obtained. This record is supported by the named author’s pinned implementation and its covariance helper, not a claim to have read that article.

The Gaussian factors remain fixed within a delayed-rejection transition. Recomputing adaptation from rejected internal candidates or ignoring reverse-path factors would require different justification.

The implementation defaults to two attempts and adaptation every 100 iterations; its usage comment about three stages is inconsistent with those executable defaults. These counts are options, not the concept identity.
Optional covariance pseudoweights, fixed nonadapted coordinates, early rejection-rate scaling, variance sampling and hierarchical updates are outside the simple fixed-target account here.

Jitter only on factorization failure differs from always adding a positive regularizer. Source-code inspection alone establishes neither correctness for arbitrary targets nor adaptive ergodicity; no MATLAB execution or performance comparison was performed.
Initialize within positive target support. Zero reverse-path probability gives zero acceptance; numerical evaluation must handle vanishing densities and log ratios without invalid divisions.

entries.name: Adaptive scaling Metropolis
entries.definition: A random-walk Metropolis algorithm that adapts its proposal scale through stochastic approximation driven by the proposal acceptance probability relative to a chosen target rate.
entries.identity_notes: The source’s ASM has fixed positive-definite shape and an adaptive scalar scale. This is distinct from covariance-shape adaptation and from RAM’s direction-dependent matrix update. The record uses the exponential-scale specialization of the source’s more general increasing scale map. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 181 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive searches of both full checkouts found prior discovery leads, neighboring sampler discussions and unrelated author-name/environment substrings. Existing random-walk Metropolis, delayed-rejection, fixed symmetric delayed-rejection and RAM records were inspected; shared components do not make these procedures equivalent.
entries.mechanism: Fix shape Sigma positive definite and use a spherical proposal W. From retained x with pi(x)>0 and log scale S, propose Y=x+exp(S)Sigma^(1/2)W. Compute alpha=min(1,pi(Y)/pi(x)), accept Y with that probability or retain x, then update S_new=S+eta_n(alpha−alpha_star). Adapt after either outcome, using the acceptance probability rather than its Bernoulli realization. Choose alpha_star in (0,1) and positive step sizes with divergent sum and convergent sum of squares for the stated stochastic-approximation setting. The shape remains fixed; exp(S) multiplies standard deviation, so the covariance multiplier is exp(2S).
entries.locator: Section 2, Assumptions 1–3 and Definition 4, PDF pp. 3–4; Theorems 7 and 9 and Remarks 11–13, pp. 5–7
limitations: The stability and strong-law theorems in this version restrict alpha_star to (0,1/2), beyond the broader algorithm definition. Larger targets are discussed as expected extensions, not proved here.

Compact-support regularity or the stated unbounded-target tail/contour assumptions and admissible proposal conditions are needed for the corresponding results. Positive step sizes alone are insufficient.
The strong-law statements concern sample averages. The source explicitly distinguishes them from convergence in distribution of the adaptive sampled states.
A target rate such as 0.234 is not a universal optimum, evidence of convergence or guarantee of good multimodal exploration.
The inspected arXiv v3 submission date and later PDF footer differ; no later journal PDF inspection or numerical validation is claimed.

entries.name: Adaptive scaling within adaptive Metropolis
entries.definition: An adaptive Metropolis algorithm that combines acceptance-rate-driven scalar proposal scaling with recursive mean and covariance-shape adaptation from retained samples.
entries.identity_notes: This record gives the bounded mean-and-shape formulation of Vihola Definition 5. Its log scale is unbounded, while the proposed mean/shape pair is accepted only inside a specified compact constraint set. Unconstrained software variants are not automatically the same validity setting. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 181 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive searches of both full checkouts found prior discovery leads, neighboring sampler discussions and unrelated author-name/environment substrings. Existing random-walk Metropolis, delayed-rejection, fixed symmetric delayed-rejection and RAM records were inspected; shared components do not make these procedures equivalent.
entries.mechanism: Choose alpha_star in (0,1) and initialize x with pi(x)>0, mu=x and feasible positive-definite Sigma. Propose Y=x+exp(S)Sigma^(1/2)W with spherical W, use alpha=min(1,pi(Y)/pi(x)), and retain X_new after the accept/reject test. Update S_new=S+eta_n(alpha−alpha_star). With the old mean mu and shape Sigma, form mu_hat=(1−eta_n)mu+eta_n X_new and Sigma_hat=(1−eta_n)Sigma+eta_n(X_new−mu)(X_new−mu)^T. For fixed zeta≥1, accept the entire proposed mean/shape pair only if ||mu_hat||≤zeta and every eigenvalue of Sigma_hat lies in [zeta^−1,zeta]; otherwise keep both old mu and old Sigma. Start with a feasible mean/shape pair and keep the scalar update separately. Use eta_n in (0,1), with divergent sum and finite squared sum under the source assumptions.
entries.locator: Section 2, Definitions 4–5 and constraint set S_zeta, PDF pp. 4–5; Theorems 7 and 9, Remarks 11–13, pp. 5–7
limitations: The covariance update uses the old mean and the retained new state, including repeated states after rejection. Substituting the new mean or only accepted proposals changes the specified recursion.
The mean and shape constraints are part of this source’s proved formulation; only the scalar scale lacks a fixed bound. Omitting constraints in practice does not inherit the same theorem.
The source’s strong-law results restrict alpha_star to (0,1/2) and require the corresponding target/proposal regularity conditions. Algorithm definition alone does not prove ergodicity.
Shape learning is a recursive stochastic-approximation update, not exactly the original unbiased full-history covariance at every finite iteration.
No universal efficiency advantage, marginal-distribution convergence or executed benchmark is asserted.

entries.name: Parallel tempering
entries.definition: A population Monte Carlo method that combines within-temperature target-preserving updates with corrected exchanges between replicas targeting differently tempered densities.
entries.identity_notes: The record identifies fixed-temperature parallel tempering, with the source’s adjacent-swap and random-walk realization as an explicit example. The population state includes all replicas; the beta=1 replica targets the original distribution. It differs from a single-chain simulated-temperature state and from adapting the temperature ladder. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 181 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive searches of both full checkouts found prior discovery leads, neighboring sampler discussions and unrelated author-name/environment substrings. Existing random-walk Metropolis, delayed-rejection, fixed symmetric delayed-rejection and RAM records were inspected; shared components do not make these procedures equivalent.
entries.mechanism: Choose a fixed L≥2 and inverse temperatures 1=beta1>...>betaL>0 for which each integral Z_beta=integral pi(x)^beta dx is finite. Initialize replicas in positive target support. The joint target is the product of pi(x_l)^beta_l/Z_beta_l. In the inspected realization, choose j uniformly from adjacent pairs and propose swapping x_j and x_(j+1), with probability min(1,[pi(x_(j+1))/pi(x_j)]^(beta_j−beta_(j+1))). Then apply a Gaussian random-walk Metropolis update at every level using acceptance min(1,[pi(y_l)/pi(x_l)]^beta_l); rejected moves retain their current replica state. Both steps preserve the joint target, so their composition does also; samples at beta1=1 have the desired stationary marginal.
entries.locator: Sections 1–2.1, Equations (1)–(10), PDF pp. 1–4; Section 2.4 implementation remarks, p. 7
limitations: All tempered densities must be normalizable; flattening a target by taking a positive power below one need not preserve integrability.
Target invariance alone does not establish irreducibility, mixing speed, finite-run convergence or independence of cold-replica samples.

The source calls the composed chain reversible. Composition of two reversible kernels need not be reversible without additional conditions; this record asserts only their directly justified invariance.
The original distribution is the cold replica’s marginal, not the pooled unweighted population distribution.
Other valid local kernels and exchange schedules require their own conditions. The record’s explicit Gaussian and adjacent-swap realization is not a claim that all implementations use it.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The paper develops adaptive parallel tempering by first defining a fixed-ladder population kernel. Temperature exchange can aid multimodal exploration, but performance examples are not universal guarantees.

entries.name: Adaptive parallel tempering
entries.definition: A parallel-tempering algorithm that adapts temperature gaps and within-replica random-walk proposal parameters through projected stochastic approximation.
entries.identity_notes: This record is the fixed-replica-count Miasojedow–Moulines–Vihola 2012 construction. Its multiplicative inverse-temperature parameterization and all-pair swap-probability updates differ from later author software using increments of reciprocal temperatures and updates for selected pairs. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 181 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Ignored-inclusive searches of both full checkouts found prior discovery leads, neighboring sampler discussions and unrelated author-name/environment substrings. Existing random-walk Metropolis, delayed-rejection, fixed symmetric delayed-rejection and RAM records were inspected; shared components do not make these procedures equivalent.
entries.mechanism: With fixed L≥2, alpha_star in (0,1) and epsilon in (0,1), set beta1=1 and beta_(l+1)=beta_l exp(−exp(rho_l)). Initialize within the parameter constraint sets and positive target support. At each iteration use the previous temperatures and proposal covariances for an adjacent exchange followed by local Gaussian Metropolis moves. From the retained post-propagation population X_new, compute every adjacent hypothetical exchange probability h_l=min(1,[pi(X_(l+1))/pi(X_l)]^(beta_l−beta_(l+1))). Update each rho_l by projection of rho_l+gamma1_n(h_l−alpha_star) onto a fixed finite interval. For each replica update mu_l=(1−gamma2_n)mu_l+gamma2_n X_new,l, and project (1−gamma2_n)Gamma_l+gamma2_n(X_new,l−mu_old,l)(X_new,l−mu_old,l)^T onto matrices with eigenvalues in [epsilon,epsilon^−1]. Update T_l by interval projection of T_l+gamma3_n(alpha_local,l−alpha_star), where alpha_local is that iteration’s local proposal acceptance probability. Use Sigma_l=exp(T_l)Gamma_l for later Gaussian proposals. Thus T is log variance, not log standard deviation; all adaptation follows the completed transition.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.3, Equations (1)–(24), PDF pp. 3–6; assumptions A1–A3 and Theorems 5 and 10, pp. 8–11
limitations: The record uses projected covariance and log-scale adaptation with separate step sequences; the mean recursion itself is not projected. Finite rho bounds keep ordered positive inverse temperatures, and the replica count is fixed.
Every rho update uses a hypothetical adjacent swap probability at the post-propagation state, not just the pair actually selected or a binary swap outcome.

The strong-law and temperature-convergence results have different hypotheses. Temperature convergence additionally needs stronger step conditions and the target solution inside the projection bounds; projection alone does not guarantee the desired rate is attainable.
The continuous-target results assume the stated tail/contour, moment and step-size conditions. Experiments omitting projections do not prove unrestricted adaptive validity.

The optional RAM proposal variant in Section 2.3 uses a physical increment where the original RAM paper uses a standardized proposal direction. That variant is excluded here; the covariance-based construction is the inspected core.
No changing-replica-count method, unrestricted adaptive convergence, universal efficiency claim or benchmark reproduction is asserted.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The paper adapts the ladder toward a common swap-acceptance target and adapts local proposals. Its validity results depend on explicit projections, regularity and step assumptions; empirical examples do not eliminate these restrictions.
